- dotnet-backend-patterns: Master C#/.NET backend development patterns for building robust APIs, MCP servers, and enterprise applications. Covers async/await, dependency injection, Entity Framework Core, Dapper, configuration, caching, and testing with xUnit. Use when developing .NET backends, reviewing C# code, or designing API architectures.
- find-skills
- kubernetes: Expert in Kubernetes and DevOps with infrastructure-as-code and cloud-native patterns
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- `Microsoft.OpenApi` is for low-level OpenAPI spec manipulation (used internally by Swashbuckle)

So the fix is to replace the `Microsoft.OpenApi` package with `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` in the project file, and keep Swashbuckle.AspNetCore which depends on the low-level OpenAPI types.

The 404 is likely because `auth-service` isn't reachable from your local machine on `localhost:8080`. The gateway proxies to `auth-service:8080` (Docker internal hostname, [ocelot.json:46-57](backend/Services/APIGateway/ocelot.json#L46-L57)).

Quick checks:
- Is `auth-service` container running? (`docker ps`)
- Is gateway running at `localhost:8080`?
- Try direct to auth-service (if exposed): `http://localhost:8080/swagger/v1/swagger.json` on auth's own port.

Also verify gateway middleware order: [Program.cs](backend/Services/APIGateway/Program.cs) needs `app.UseRouting()` + `await app.UseOcelot()` — it has both, but `UseOcelot()` must come after routing. If still 404, Ocelot isn't matching; check auth-service is healthy at `http://auth-service:8080/health`.

content.text:
You're using **Helm** — there's no raw `Deployment` for kubectl to restart. To redeploy with latest images:

```powershell
# Restart cue-services release
helm upgrade cue-services ./infra/helm/cue-services --namespace cue --timeout 5m

# Or just force a new rollout by upgrading with the same chart
helm upgrade cue-services ./infra/helm/cue-services --namespace cue --set image.tag=latest --timeout 5m
```

If images are tagged with a new build SHA and you just want to pick them up:

```powershell
helm template cue-services ./infra/helm/cue-services | kubectl apply -f - -n cue
# or
helm upgrade cue-services ./infra/helm/cue-services --namespace cue --timeout 5m --wait
```

Check the Helm chart values to see how image tags are configured — likely there's an `image.tag` or `global.imageTag` that needs updating to match your latest build.

I ran this but the pods are not pulling latest images
helm upgrade cue-services .\helm-chart-services\  --namespace cue --timeout 5m

Your pods aren't pulling new images because Helm is using the same image digest as before. The containers were rebuilt locally, but Kubernetes doesn't know that — it just sees the same `image` tag/reference and skips the pull (unless `Always`).

content.text:
Your chart uses `IfNotPresent` with `imageTag: latest`. Kubernetes skips pull if `latest` already exists locally — so pods never restart with rebuilt images.

Force it:
```powershell
# Option 1: Set pull policy + rollout
helm upgrade cue-services .\helm-chart-services\ --namespace cue --timeout 5m --set global.imagePullPolicy=Always,backend.imageTag=latest
```

Or directly delete pods to force recreation:
```powershell
# Option 2: Delete pods (they recreate with fresh pulls)
kubectl delete pods -n cue -l app.kubernetes.io/name=auth-service
# ... or all backend pods
```

Or edit chart/deployment to set `imagePullPolicy: Always`:

Now I can see the values file clearly. The issue is clear:

1. `imageTag: latest` 
2. `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`

Since the image tag is `latest` (a mutable tag), Kubernetes will skip pulling if the image already exists on the node. This is why pods aren't picking up the rebuilt images.

There are a few ways to fix this:

1. **Change to `imagePullPolicy: Always`** - but this is inefficient in production
2. **Use unique image tags** - best practice (e.g., git commit SHA, build number, timestamp)
3. **Delete pods manually** - forces recreation and pull


4. **Override the pull policy during helm upgrade** - I can pass `--set global.imagePullPolicy=Always` to force a fresh pull without modifying the chart

The most pragmatic approach here is option 3 - manually deleting the pods to trigger recreation with the updated image.

Actually, I should also consider what's happening with the Docker images themselves. The user ran `helm upgrade` locally, which rebuilds the local Docker images, but Kubernetes clusters might not automatically pull those latest images unless the image pull policy is set to `Always`. The safest fix is to either delete the pods directly to force recreation, or pass the `--set global.imagePullPolicy=Always` flag to the helm upgrade command to ensure all services pull the latest images.

Found it: **`pull access denied for auth-service, repository does not exist or may require 'docker login'`**

Kubernetes is looking in Docker Hub for `auth-service:latest` etc. But your local k3s setup likely uses a different registry (or `imagePullPolicy: Always` is now hitting a registry that doesn't have these names). For a **local k3s** setup, images are usually loaded via `k3s ctr images import` or built with a local registry.

Two options:

**Option 1 — Disable pull (use locally-loaded images)**
```powershell
helm upgrade cue-services .\helm-chart-services\ --namespace cue -f .\helm-chart-services\values-local.yaml --set global.imagePullPolicy=Never
```
This uses whatever is already in the k3s containerd.

**Option 2 — Build & import directly into k3s**
```powershell
# For each service, save docker image and import
docker build -t auth-service:latest .\src\backend\Services\AuthService
docker save auth-service:latest | sudo k3s ctr images import -
```

Since the older pods ran fine, you already have these images in k3s. **Option 1 is fastest** — revert pull policy to `Never` (or `IfNotPresent`) and the pods will use cached images. But that means: when you rebuild, you also need to `docker save | k3s ctr images import` to refresh the cache.

content.text:
Found the issue. From [APIGateway/Program.cs:48](backend/Services/APIGateway/Program.cs#L48):

```csharp
app.UseHttpsRedirection();   // line 48
```

When the gateway proxies to `auth-service` and gets a response, it tries to **redirect HTTPS** on the way out — but the response has already started (headers sent). The redirect middleware throws `ReasonPhrase cannot be set because the response has already started.` and Ocelot catches it as a 500.

Two fixes — pick one:

**Option 1 (cleanest)**: Remove `app.UseHttpsRedirection()` from APIGateway (gateways usually stay HTTP internally; TLS terminates at the LB/ingress, not the app).

Root cause found. **`System.MissingMethodException: 'IOpenApiRequestBody.get_Content()'`** — `Swashbuckle.AspNetCore 10.2.3` was built against a newer version of `Microsoft.OpenApi` and the runtime can't find the API.

Your [AuthService.csproj](backend/Services/AuthService/AuthService.csproj) has:
```xml
<PackageReference Include="Swashbuckle.AspNetCore" Version="10.2.3" />
<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.OpenApi" Version="3.10.2" />
```

`Swashbuckle 10.2.3` requires `Microsoft.OpenApi >= 11.0` (the API surface changed). The cached `3.10.2` doesn't have the new method.

Fix: bump `Microsoft.OpenApi` in **all services** to a compatible version (11.x):
```powershell
# Update all csproj files
"backend/Services/*/*.csproj" | ForEach-Object { (Get-Content $_) -replace '<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.OpenApi" Version="3.10.2" />', '<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.OpenApi" Version="11.0.0" />' | Set-Content $_ }
```

Or just check NuGet for the version that matches Swashbuckle 10.2.3:
- 10.2.3 may be paired with `Microsoft.OpenApi` `2.7.5` (which the gateway's earlier restore error complained about) — that's actually the transitive version.

**Cleaner fix**: just remove the explicit `Microsoft.OpenApi` reference from `AuthService.csproj` — let Swashbuckle's transitively-required version win.

Now rebuild auth-service and gateway with the corrected references (Swashbuckle's transitively-pulled `Microsoft.OpenApi` will be the one that matches the API surface):

```powershell
# Rebuild auth-service
docker build --no-cache -t auth-service:latest -f backend/Services/AuthService/Dockerfile .
docker save auth-service:latest | k3s ctr images import -

# Rebuild api-gateway
docker build --no-cache -t api-gateway:latest -f backend/Services/APIGateway/Dockerfile .
docker save api-gateway:latest | k3s ctr images import -

# Recreate pods
kubectl delete pod -n cue $(kubectl get pods -n cue --no-headers | grep -E "auth-service|api-gateway" | awk '{print $1}') --ignore-not-found
```

The gateway's `SwaggerGen` registers `auth`, `user`, etc. as **doc names** — but the gateway has no controllers with those routes. The actual proxying should be done by Ocelot for `/swagger/auth/swagger.json` path.

- Line 48: `UseRouting`
